  - the score prices the Separation violation, but no attempt can ever reduce it

A rule that nothing can act on is a rule that only generates noise. The Separation rule is correct and well-designed — it already measures hardware-to-hardware using each part's panel offset rather than placement origins, which is the subtle part — but it is being applied at the wrong STAGE.

The overlap originates in the AUTO-DERIVED panel: derive_panel / min_panel_hp spaced these two cutouts closer than their envelopes allow. That is where it must be enforced, because that is the last point at which anything can still move.

WANTED: run the Separation check during panel derivation, against CutoutSpec::envelope_mm, and either space the cutouts to satisfy it or refuse and report. A derived panel that cannot be assembled should not be silently substituted for the declared one (see [[legion-of-bom-m1b]], which is how this board came to be built at 6 HP in the first place).

Related: [[legion-of-bom-cll.5]] wants the same figure live while dragging in the placement editor, and [[legion-of-bom-tvs]] (toggle cutout is 6.5mm, real sub-mini toggles need 4.95mm) suggests SW1's envelope may itself be wrong — worth checking before tuning spacing.

title: [epic] Layout rules that mean something electrically — and that the placer must obey
description:
PROFILES ARE THE ORGANISING IDEA. A design rule is not universally true — it is true FOR A CLASS OF BOARD. Controlled impedance and return-path discontinuity are load-bearing on a digital board and meaningless on an audio-band OTA circuit; high-impedance-node length and star grounding are the reverse. One undifferentiated rule set can only be the intersection (uselessly thin) or the union (confidently wrong on every board).

THE CONCEPT IS HALF-BUILT ALREADY. LayoutMode { Analog, Digital, Mixed } exists in layout.rs and is plumbed from the CLI (lob fab --mode). But it produces ONLY CostWeights — grep rules.rs for LayoutMode and there are zero hits. So today the profile changes how the optimiser WEIGHS a placement and has no say in WHICH RULES EXIST. That is the gap this epic closes.

The seam is already cut: rules::derive_in takes a Context (facts, outline). The profile belongs there, and derive_in decides which rules to emit.

WHY IT MATTERS NOW. Two days of measurement on the slew limiter kept landing on the same shape of problem: the thing that actually broke the board was never expressed as a rule, so nothing could see it, score it, or repair it.

  - The cross-side through-hole collision that killed the -12V net ([[legion-of-bom-ude]]) lived ONLY inside board::placement_clear. Not a Rule, so legalize could not repair it, the score could not price it, and the dashboard rules panel never mentioned it. Six connections unroutable by any router while every gate reported "all design rules met".
  - summing::snap ([[legion-of-bom-6yh]]) is the inverse mistake: an objective as a code path that OVERRIDES placement, so it cannot be traded off. Measured, it costs 5 DRC errors and 2 connections.
  - The panel Separation rule is unenforceable when both parts are anchored: RV2 and SW1 overlap by 7.23 x 5.51mm and nothing can move either.

rules.rs already states the principle ("a rule is a record, not a code path... adding a rule means adding a variant and a deriver, not editing the placer") and the caution ("a rule measures what a placement can see, which is rarely the quantity that matters — name the proxy"). This epic closes the gap between those two sentences, and adds the third: say which BOARDS each rule is true of.

PROFILE SKETCH, to be argued not assumed:
  - Analog (audio band, +/-12V, our modules today): high-impedance node length, decoupling loop area, PSRR/supply routing, keeping CV inputs clear of the power header, panel-hardware separation.
  - Digital (arrives with the Daisy, [[legion-of-bom-25z]]): return-path continuity under the pour, via stitching at plane transitions, controlled impedance where it applies, crystal/clock keep-outs.
  - Mixed: partition + the join point, which is exactly what MT-031 is about.
  - Physical/manufacturing rules (edge clearance, courtyard overlap, drill-to-edge) are PROFILE-INDEPENDENT and come from IPC-2221. Getting this split right is most of the work.

SOURCES, scoped by profile rather than dismissed wholesale — the earlier framing here said "high-speed SI does not apply" and that was too blunt. It does not apply to the ANALOG profile; it is the digital profile's core literature.
  - Analog: Analog Devices MT-031 (Kester/Bryant/Byrne); AD Analog Dialogue decoupling tutorial (2017); Henry Ott, Electromagnetic Compatibility Engineering (Wiley 2009).
  - Digital/mixed: Eric Bogatin, Signal and Power Integrity Simplified; Johnson & Graham, High-Speed Digital Design.
  - Profile-independent: IPC-2221, the one that is genuinely machine-readable.

title: summing::snap makes the board measurably worse — 5 DRC errors and 2 unrouted, and it is the last impossible-by-placement connection
description:
MEASURED 2026-07-28 on the real puget-hardware slew limiter, by toggling the pass and changing nothing else. Same placement, same router, same panel:

                        unrouted   DRC   impossible-by-placement
  with summing::snap        4        7            1
  without                   2        2            0
  (gridrouter, with)        7       10
  (gridrouter, without)     4        4

lob fab gate: 7 DRC / 4 unrouted WITH  ->  2 DRC / 2 unrouted WITHOUT.

The pass costs 5 DRC errors and 2 connections, and it is the sole cause of the last "impossible by placement" connection (RATE_CV -> RV1.2). Both remaining errors without it are unconnected_items: +12V -> U2.4 and SIG_IN -> U2.3.

IT NO LONGER EARNS ITS KEEP. summing::snap was landed under [[legion-of-bom-yck]] to make CTRL_FB and CTRL_SUM routable, and it did. But with the through-hole collision bug fixed ([[legion-of-bom-ude]]), NEITHER net appears in the unrouted list with the pass disabled — they route fine without it. The likeliest reading is that the original CTRL_FB/CTRL_SUM failure was the same cross-side THT collision all along, and the snap was treating the symptom rather than the cause.

IT ALSO HAS THE BUG ude FIXED. summing.rs has zero occupancy checks (grep for overlap/occupied/collide/clash returns nothing). Its pinned argument only stops PINNED parts being moved; it does not stop other parts being moved ON TOP of them. So it can drop a passive onto a panel control's through-hole pad exactly as decouple::snap did.

RECOMMENDATION: delete the pass, or gate it behind the same first_overlap guard decouple::snap now uses and re-measure. Deleting is the honest default — a pass that costs 5 DRC errors and whose original justification no longer reproduces is not carrying its weight. Keep the module doc as the record of what was learned about summing-node placement.

REPRODUCE: a temporary LOB_NO_SUMMING env gate in board.rs (do not ship it) plus crates/core/examples/route_bench.rs.
close_reason: summing::snap removed from the pipeline in board.rs; module and its reasoning kept as the record. Guarding it with the shared first_overlap occupancy check (the fix that rescued decouple::snap) changed nothing — 7 DRC / 4 unrouted with the guard, same as without — so the harm was never collisions. It is that a pass which OVERRIDES placement cannot be traded off, and so wins even when measured to cost five DRC errors. Objective moves to the score: [[legion-of-bom-tsy.3]]. Slew limiter went 7 DRC / 4 unrouted -> 2 / 2 on removal, then 0 / 0 with the router budget raised.

title: PathfinderRouter landed (negotiated congestion) — better router, but not the slew limiter's blocker
description:
Implements PathFinder (McMurchie & Ebeling, FPGA'95) as a Router alongside GridRouter. crates/core/src/route.rs.

HOW IT WORKS. Phase 1 negotiates: every iteration rips up and reroutes EVERY net, and nets are allowed to overlap — overlap is priced, not forbidden. Present congestion rises with occupancy and with a factor that grows each round; history accumulates on cells that stay contested and never decays, which is what stops two nets swapping into the same corridor forever. Phase 2 spends what was learned: the same hard-clearance ordering search GridRouter uses, but nets ordered most-contested-first and biased by the history map. Copper that ships is legal by construction — negotiation state is never emitted.

Shared machinery so the two are comparable: build_surface() discretises the board identically for both, and route_pass() is now a free function taking a congestion bias (a neutral one reduces the arithmetic to exactly the old unbiased cost, so GridRouter is unchanged — its 11 tests still pass).

MEASURED on the real puget-hardware slew limiter, same placement both sides (crates/core/examples/route_bench.rs, max_iters=1 so placement repair cannot mask the router):

  declared panel, 6 HP:  unrouted 4->2,  DRC 8->6
  declared panel, 8 HP:  unrouted 16->14, DRC 9->6
  declared panel, 10 HP: tie (20/14 both)
  auto panel (what fab builds, 6 HP): unrouted 10->9, DRC 16->15

So it is a real improvement to the router — better or tied on every width tried, with less copper and fewer vias.

BUT END-TO-END IT IS A WASH. Through lob fab (layout loop, 6 placement attempts) PathFinder gives 13 DRC / 6 unrouted against GridRouter's 12 / 5 — marginally WORSE, because a different placement attempt wins the loop's scoring. Runtime 43s, acceptable.

DEFAULT NOT CHANGED. BoardOptions still uses GridRouter, deliberately and with a comment saying why: shipping a one-error regression on the flagship board to land an algorithm is the wrong trade. Switching it is a decision to make once the placement/router interaction is understood.

THE REAL CONCLUSION, and it is the useful one: routing was NOT the slew limiter's blocker. A materially better router moves the board from 12 DRC errors to 13. The failure is upstream — see [[legion-of-bom-e7k]] (RANGE switch) and [[legion-of-bom-qng]].

comments.author: Avery Wagar
comments.text:
CORRECTION 2026-07-27. The earlier writeup on this bead — 'better router, end-to-end a wash, default not changed' — was measuring MY BUGS, not the algorithm. User pushed back that a peer-reviewed, universally-deployed algorithm being barely better was more likely a bad implementation than a bad algorithm. They were right. Three defects, found by instrumenting the negotiation loop:

1. PRESENT SWAMPED HISTORY BY ~300,000x. p_fac grew 2x per round and was capped at 1<<22, so it reached ~4,200,000x base cost by round 14. History — the term that is supposed to SETTLE the negotiation — could only ever reach ~13x. Instrumented overused-cell counts showed exactly what that looks like: 301, 196, 170, 131, 46, 19, 24, 27, 19, 19, 14, 11, 10, 24, 33, 24, 8, 11, 30, 9, 16, 4, 7, 12 — 24 rounds of thrash, never settling, best round (4) thrown away. Fixed: growth 2.0 -> 1.3 (VPR's figure), cap 1<<22 -> 64x, history step 0.5 -> 1.0.

2. THE NEGOTIATED SOLUTION WAS DISCARDED. When PathFinder converges, the routes ARE the answer — legal by construction. I threw them away unconditionally and re-routed from scratch with the greedy router, keeping only the net order and history map. That is not PathFinder; that is using PathFinder as a hint generator. Fixed: track the best round by (unreached, overused), and when it is legal, emit it.

3. NO 'NEVER WORSE' GUARD. Steering the fallback with a history map from a negotiation that never settled made it LOSE to the plain router (0 conflicts -> 1) on a board GridRouter handles. Fixed: run the unbiased search too and keep the guided result only when it actually won. Now a code property with a regression test.

Also: my first discriminating test had both nets' pads at IDENTICAL coordinates, so those cells were Cell::Blocked and the board was unroutable by construction — it was measuring nothing, and I weakened its assertion instead of fixing it when it failed to discriminate.

RE-MEASURED after the fixes, same placement both sides:
  auto panel (what lob fab builds): unrouted 10->7, DRC 16->13, copper -109.5mm, vias -5   [was -1/-1]
  declared panel 6 HP: tie on unrouted/DRC, copper -67mm, vias -5
  declared panel 8 HP: unrouted tie, DRC 9->7, copper -127mm, vias -9

END TO END through lob fab: 12 DRC / 5 unrouted — TIED with GridRouter, up from 13/6. DEFAULT NOW SWITCHED to PathfinderRouter: strictly better at fixed placement, tied at the gate, and ~110mm less copper with 5 fewer vias, which is a real manufacturing gain at equal DRC.

The conclusion about the slew limiter is UNCHANGED and still holds: a correctly-implemented negotiated-congestion router does not unblock this board. What did change is that the router is now actually good, and the earlier claim that the algorithm underperformed was wrong.

title: Mouser search API intermittently reports throttling as 'Invalid API Key' — retries are swallowed as 'part not found'
description:
CORRECTED 2026-07-27. An earlier reading of this said the stored MOUSER_API_KEY was dead. THAT WAS WRONG — the key is valid. Do not go issue a new one.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS. The same key, same endpoint, same part number returns success or an auth error depending on call spacing:

  POST /api/v1/search/partnumber, mouserPartNumber=667-ERJ-2RKF1003X
    -> Errors: [], NumberOfResult: 1, 1289405 In Stock          (spaced call)
    -> {"Code":"Invalid","Message":"Invalid unique identifier.",
        "ResourceKey":"InvalidIdentifier","PropertyName":"API Key"}   (rapid call)

Four MPNs queried back-to-back failed 4/4. The same four, spaced 4-10s with retry, resolved. So Mouser throttles and reports the throttle as a CREDENTIAL error against PropertyName 'API Key'.

WHY IT BITES. crate::mouser treats a non-empty Errors[] as a failed lookup, so a throttled call is indistinguishable from 'no such part'. A priced BOM silently comes back unpriced, and suggest_mpns silently returns nothing — both read as 'Mouser does not carry this', which is the exact opposite of the truth. That misreading is what produced the wrong diagnosis above, so it has already cost real time once.

WANTED:
1. Retry with backoff on ResourceKey == InvalidIdentifier rather than treating it as terminal.
2. Distinguish the three outcomes in the type: found / genuinely-absent / could-not-ask. Today the last two collapse, and only the last is worth retrying.
3. Rate-limit outbound calls — a BOM lookup walks every line, which is precisely the burst that trips this.

VERIFIED WORKING once spaced (2026-07-27), while sourcing [[2opfm-50-board-run-jul-2026]]:
  VAOL-3LAE2        -> 593-VAOL-3LAE2,        VCC,    1747 in stock, lead 112d
  PTA2043-2015DPB103 -> 652-PTA2432015DPB103, Bourns, 1073 in stock, lead 98d
  WQP-WQP518MA       -> 0 results (genuinely not a Mouser part)
  RV9012NO-PA25B7.0  -> 0 results (genuinely not a Mouser part)

title: Spacing tools: set pitch, distribute evenly, make column/row/grid, break pattern
description:
SPACING — the other tool the user asked for by name, and the one that produces
the file format's real value.

  * SET PITCH on a selection: they become evenly spaced at exactly N mm. This
    IS [[patterns.column]] pitch / [[patterns.row]] pitch — the operation and
    the file format are the same thing.
  * DISTRIBUTE EVENLY between the two outermost parts (pitch derived, not
    given).
  * MAKE COLUMN / MAKE ROW / MAKE GRID from a selection: infer the axis from
    how the parts currently sit, infer a starting pitch, then let it be typed
    exactly. A grid takes cols + pitch_x + pitch_y and fills across-then-down,
    which is how PlacementFile::positions already expands it.
  * BREAK PATTERN: expand back to explicit [controls] entries when the strip
    stops being a strip.
  * common Eurorack pitches offered as presets, since these are the numbers
    people actually use for jack strips — read them off the shipped
    slew_limiter_panel.toml rather than inventing them.

The test that this is right: after "make column, pitch 13.5", the TOML contains
one [[patterns.column]] table with three refdes and a pitch — not three
[controls] entries 13.5mm apart. Round-tripping a placement through the editor
must not increase the file's entropy.
close_reason: Spacing. Set pitch, Distribute (pitch derived from the outermost pair), Make column / Make row (forcing the axis Set pitch infers), Make grid with a cols field, Break (BreakPattern op added to the writer: expands a pattern to explicit controls at the positions it already produces, so nothing moves), Rejoin (ClearControl). Pitch presets are HP multiples plus the 16mm jack pitch the shipped slew_limiter_panel.toml actually uses — not invented numbers. The pitch field prefills from the selection's current spacing. Verified: after 'make column, pitch 13.5' the TOML holds one [[patterns.column]] with three refdes, no [controls] entries.

title: Alignment tools: align/centre/mirror + snapping to HP grid, part edges, panel margins
description:
ALIGNMENT — one of the two tools the user asked for by name.

Operations on a selection, all of them writing through the placement writer:
  * align left / right / centre on X
  * align top / bottom / centre on Y
  * centre on the PANEL's horizontal axis — the common one for a single column
    of jacks, and the one people eyeball wrongly
  * mirror a selection about the panel centreline

SNAPPING, which is most of what makes alignment feel good:
  * to the Eurorack HP grid (5.08mm) and to half-HP
  * to another part's X or Y (the guide line appears while dragging)
  * to a fixed margin from the panel edge
  * snapping is a modifier away from being off — hold to disable, because the
    one time you need 0.3mm off-grid the tool must not fight you

An alignment applied to parts in a pattern should update the PATTERN
(x, from_y) rather than exploding it into N [controls] entries. That is the
whole point of the file format and the easiest thing to get wrong: the file
should still say "a column at x=6.0" afterwards, not list five coordinates that
happen to share an x.
close_reason: Alignment + snapping. Tools: align left/centre-X/right, top/middle/bottom, centre on the panel axis, mirror about the panel centreline. All route through core ops_for_targets, so aligning a strip's x updates the PATTERN (file still says 'a column at x=9.0') instead of exploding into N controls — the case the issue names, pinned by a test. Snapping while dragging: HP and half-HP grid, other parts' x/y with a guide line, panel centreline, and the part's own envelope from each edge (a derived margin rather than an invented fixed one — noted as a deviation). Alt disables snapping.

title: Drag + multi-select panel parts on the board render (panel-space, keyboard nudge)
description:
The canvas: hit-test, select, drag the PANEL parts on the board render the
dashboard already draws.

Scope is deliberately only the parts with panel cutouts (jacks, pots, switches,
LEDs) — the ones BuiltinCutouts recognises and the ones a person has an opinion
about. Everything else stays where the placer put it and is drawn dimmed.

  * click to select, shift/marquee for multi-select
  * drag one or many, in panel-space mm, with the live position readout
  * arrow keys nudge by 0.1mm, shift-arrow by 1mm — a knob 0.4mm off centre is
    a real defect and mouse precision will not find it
  * escape/undo, because a mis-drag on a 5-part panel is otherwise expensive

Dragging a part that belongs to a pattern is the interesting case: either it
leaves the pattern (becomes a [controls] override) or it MOVES the pattern.
Decide deliberately and make it visible in the UI — this is the difference
between a tool that keeps intent and one that quietly shreds it.
close_reason: Canvas landed. New GET /api/circuits/{name}/controls serves the built board in panel space (core placement::board_view, computed exactly as panel_from_board does so the editor and the derived panel agree to the micron). SPA crates/web/web/src/placement.tsx draws an SVG in panel mm: panel hardware draggable with its hole + envelope, board internals dimmed for context. Click/shift/marquee select, drag, arrows 0.1mm and shift-arrows 1mm, esc abandons a drag, cmd-Z undo / shift-cmd-Z redo, cmd-A select all. The pattern question is decided AND visible: a covered pattern moves as a pattern (chip says 'column of 3'); a partly-selected one warns 'J2 will leave its pattern'. Also warns when controls have moved since the last build, since the board follows the placement.

title: placement.toml writer + web endpoint (format-preserving, re-parse to validate)
description:
FOUNDATION — nothing else in this epic can persist without it.

A format-preserving writer for `<circuit>.placement.toml`, modelled directly on
crate::panel_edit: edit through toml_edit so comments, key order and untouched
tables survive the round-trip, then RE-PARSE as PlacementFile so a malformed
edit fails loudly instead of corrupting the file the board is built from.

Operations the UI needs (this is the whole API surface):
  * set an explicit control position          -> [controls] refdes = {x, y}
  * create/replace a pattern                  -> [[patterns.column|row|grid]]
  * remove a refdes from a pattern            (it becomes a [controls] entry, or
                                               the pattern shrinks — decide and
                                               document which)
  * delete an override so a part rejoins its pattern

MUST PRESERVE THE ESCAPE HATCH already specified in crate::placement: a
[controls] entry overrides the pattern that produced it, and that is the
documented way to nudge one part out of a strip without unpicking the strip.
PlacementFile::positions() already errors when two PATTERNS claim the same
refdes but treats an explicit control as legal — keep exactly that asymmetry.

Coordinates are PANEL SPACE (mm from the panel's bottom-left), which is how the
file reads and how a person thinks about a front panel. The board-frame flip
lives in PlacementFile::anchors and must not be duplicated here.

Plus the POST endpoint in crates/web, following /api/edit's shape, and a write
guard: refuse to write a placement that names a refdes not in the circuit.
close_reason: Writer + endpoint landed. crates/core/src/placement_edit.rs: format-preserving toml_edit writer with 6 ops (SetControl/ClearControl/SetColumn/SetRow/SetGrid/DropFromPattern), batch-applied in order, re-parsed as PlacementFile AND expanded through positions() before returning. Write guard takes a required &HashSet<String> of the circuit's refdes. Escape-hatch asymmetry preserved exactly. crates/web/src/placement.rs: GET+POST /api/circuits/{name}/placement, staging like /api/edit. 20 core tests + 5 route tests.

title: [epic] Control-surface placement editor — place panel hardware in our UI with alignment + spacing tools
description:
Hand-place the CONTROL SURFACE in our own dashboard, not KiCad — with real
alignment and spacing tools — and let the machine keep the board internals.

WHY OUR UI AND NOT KICAD. KiCad gives you coordinates. crate::placement's
PlacementFile stores INTENT:

    [[patterns.column]]
    refdes = ["J1", "J2", "J4"]
    x = 6.0
    from_y = 10.5
    pitch = 13.5

"These three jacks are a column on 13.5mm pitch." Change the pitch and they all
move; change HP and the column stays coherent. Drag the same jacks in KiCad and
you get three (x,y) pairs with the reason discarded — which is why capturing a
KiCad layout is the fallback (see the capture child) and not the plan. The
alignment and spacing tools ARE this file format, exposed as operations.

THE SPLIT THIS EPIC DEPENDS ON. Two different jobs, and conflating them is what
makes placement UIs miserable:
  * CONTROL SURFACE — 5-8 panel parts (jacks, pots, switches). Ergonomics, human
    judgement, needs alignment. THE USER PLACES THESE. This epic.
  * BOARD INTERNALS — 40-odd passives. Nobody hand-places 0603s. The placer owns
    these, then crate::decouple and crate::summing do the pin-level work they
    are now measurably good at.

WHY NOW. The auto-placer cannot make an ergonomics decision and never will —
crate::placement says so in its own docs: "a fine starting point and a bad final
answer, because panel ergonomics are a design decision and no cost function has
an opinion about it." And the flagship board is not shippable
([[legion-of-bom-qng]]), so the fastest route to a real product is the human
placing the 6 parts that need judgement.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS, so this is assembly rather than invention:
  * PlacementFile schema + pattern expansion + panel-space<->board flip, tested
  * crate::panel_edit — the format-preserving toml_edit writer pattern, with a
    deliberate allowlist boundary and re-parse-to-validate
  * the dashboard already POSTs (/api/edit, /circuits/{name}/build) — not
    read-only any more
  * the PCB render in the dashboard (PCB/Panel/Schematic, Top/Bottom)
  * rules::assess returns per-part margins, and the dashboard already renders
    "Design rules — N of M broken"
  * `<circuit>.placement.toml` is ALREADY read by the CLI and already WINS over
    the panel spec's cutouts, deliberately

COHERENCE CONSTRAINT — do not break this. placement.toml overrides the panel's
anchors; the board follows the placement; the panel is then derived back from
the board (panel::panel_from_board). That is what stops the panel and the board
drifting apart. Anything here writes placement.toml and lets that chain run —
never write cutout positions directly. Note effective_panel substitutes a
derived panel when the declared one is stale ([[legion-of-bom-m1b]]); check the
interaction before shipping.

title: Ship a fab-capability .kicad_dru with the board so DRC checks JLCPCB limits, not KiCad defaults
description:
Our generated boards declare essentially NO design rules. The (setup) block is:

    (setup (pad_to_mask_clearance 0) (aux_axis_origin ...))

No clearances, no track/via minimums, no (rules). So every DRC number this
project has ever quoted was measured against KiCad's BUILT-IN DEFAULTS, not
against what JLCPCB can actually make. The gate has been checking the wrong
standard -- not a wrong answer, an unrelated question.

VERIFIED THE MECHANISM WORKS: kicad-cli honours a sibling <board>.kicad_dru.
Probe -- dropped a deliberately absurd rule next to a board:
    (rule "PROBE" (constraint edge_clearance (min 5mm)) (condition "A.Type=='track'"))
DRC went 0 errors -> 17 copper_edge_clearance. So writing a .kicad_dru beside the
board in the fab package is enough; no KiCad project file needed.

THEN JUDGED OUR OWN "CLEAN" BOARD AGAINST REAL JLCPCB NUMBERS (2-layer, values
transcribed from labtroll/KiCad-DesignRules):
    track_width 0.127 / clearance 0.127 / edge_clearance 0.3 / hole 0.2..6.3 /
    annular 0.075 / hole_to_hole 0.5 / silk_clearance 0.15 /
    text_thickness 0.15 / text_height 1.0

    RESULT: 0 errors, 228 warnings.

  The copper is genuinely fine -- our router's defaults (0.25mm trace, 0.2mm
  clearance, 0.8/0.4 via => 0.2mm annular) sit comfortably inside every JLCPCB
  minimum. That is a real result and worth knowing.
  The silkscreen is not -- see [[legion-of-bom-2gy]].

WHERE TO STEAL FROM (all .kicad_dru, all JLCPCB-targeted):
  * https://github.com/labtroll/KiCad-DesignRules   -- KiCad 7, clean single
    file, the numeric table above came from it
  * https://github.com/Cimos/KiCad-CustomDesignRules -- KiCad 8, JLCPCB AND
    PCBWay, validated against a paired test board
  * https://github.com/tinfever/KiCAD-Custom-DRC-Rules-for-JLCPCB-with-Unit-Tests
    -- selectable 2-layer/4-layer/2oz variants with PASS/FAIL test boards per
    rule. Closest in spirit to how this repo works.
  * https://github.com/ziteh/kicad-design-rules

  CHECK THE LICENCE BEFORE VENDORING -- none of the ones inspected stated one in
  the README. Transcribing the numeric limits from a manufacturer's published
  capability sheet is the safer route than copying a file wholesale.

WHAT NONE OF THEM SOLVES: not one has a footprint-inside-the-board-outline rule,
because KiCad's constraint vocabulary cannot express it (see
[[legion-of-bom-670]]). crate::rules Tier::Physical stays regardless.

SCOPE: emit <stem>.kicad_dru into the fab package next to <stem>.kicad_pcb, pick
the rule set from the board's layer count + the kit/process, and let the existing
DRC gate do the rest. The numbers should live next to the other JLCPCB knowledge
in crate::jlcpcb, which today has no capability data at all.

comments.author: Avery Wagar
comments.text: Correction: the silkscreen bead is [[legion-of-bom-0rt]], not 2gy (id guessed before filing).

title: slew_limiter at 5 HP is not fab-ready: 6 DRC errors incl. an unrouted critical net
description:
The state of the actual product board, measured cleanly (greedy placer, current
loop, KiCad DRC as the gate) on 2026-07-26:

  score 1581.2, rule penalty 0 (all design rules met)
  6 KiCad DRC errors:
      3x unconnected_items
      1x courtyards_overlap
      1x shorting_items
      1x solder_mask_bridge
  and one of those unrouted nets is CRITICAL: SLEW_NODE cannot reach U1.7.

`lob fab` refuses this, correctly. This is the board that matters and it is not
shippable -- while every demo circuit in the legion-of-bom repo builds 0-DRC.
A whole session was spent moving demo-board SCORES (a wirelength/via proxy) by
5-20% while this sat at 6 errors. Worth stating plainly: the score is a
preference proxy, DRC is the gate, and only the gate decides whether a board
can be built.

Likely the same root as [[legion-of-bom-e7k]] (slew limiter does not route clean
with the RANGE switch) and related to [[legion-of-bom-yck]] (router leaves nets
unrouted on dense 2-layer boards). 5 HP may simply be too tight for this part
count -- the shipped board was 8 HP -- in which case the answer is either more
HP or a real rip-up router, not placement tuning.

comments.author: Avery Wagar
comments.text:
ROOT-CAUSED, and it is NOT a width problem. It is [[legion-of-bom-yck]], and the
measurement now proves it.

WIDTH SWEEP (hp_search, real place -> route -> KiCad DRC per width, on the actual
puget-hardware netlist, with the greedy placer restored):

     6 HP · 12 DRC errors (9x unconnected)     <- geometric floor
     8 HP ·  5 DRC errors (4x unconnected)
    10 HP ·  4 DRC errors (4x unconnected)
    nothing in range built clean

Nearly doubling the board area takes unconnected from 9 to 4 and then STOPS. At
8 HP and 10 HP the failures are byte-identical:

    CTRL_FB  could not route to pad U2.13
    CTRL_SUM could not route to pad U2.12

Two connections, same two at every width. More copper does not help.

WHY. Measured on the 8 HP build:
    CTRL_SUM = RA.2, RB.2, U2.12 — RA sits 44.8mm from U2 pin 12
    CTRL_FB  = RF.1, RG.1, U2.13 — RF ~19mm away
That is the summing-amp feedback network scattered the length of the board, which
is precisely what yck measured ("RA 45.45mm") and precisely why: RA is on
RATE_CV (at RV1, top of board) as well as CTRL_SUM (at U2), so a centroid placer
puts it halfway between. U2 pins 12/13/14 are the TL074's section D — 13 is the
inverting input, a virtual-ground summing node.

RULED OUT along the way:
  * width (above)
  * pad-to-pad clearance geometry on the SOIC-14 — the 1.27mm pitch leaves a
    0.67mm gap and the router's halo is 0.325mm a side, which is marginal, but
    rebuilding at 0.20mm trace / 0.15mm clearance changes NOTHING. Same two nets.
  * the placer swap — greedy and analytical both scatter RA the same way.

THE FIX is the one yck already specified and nobody has built: a snap pass for
high-impedance summing nodes, shaped like crate::decouple::snap — take the
placement as given and move the passives onto the specific PIN they feed. Not a
pull, not an adjacency weight: two attempts at those have now failed (FEEDBACK_
PULL went 5 DRC -> 7 and was reverted; analytical placement broke a physical rule
and was reverted in [[legion-of-bom-10k]]). "Against this pin" is a position.

INGREDIENTS CONFIRMED PRESENT: SymbolGraphics::pin_names (symbols.rs:456) carries
the "-" pin name, PartFacts::pin_offsets (board.rs:91) carries the pad geometry,
and decouple::snap is the working template for exactly this shape of pass.

comments.author: Avery Wagar
comments.text:
The two blocking connections are FIXED by [[legion-of-bom-yck]]'s snap pass (crate::summing, c93bab4). Re-measured, unconnected nets: 6 HP 9->5, 8 HP 4->2, 10 HP 4->1. At 10 HP the board is now ONE unconnected net (N$3 -> U2.9) and one DRC error from clean — it was 4 and 4.

This also reframes the width question. Widening never helped before because the failure was topological; now that it is fixed, width does buy something: 10 HP is close to clean while 6 HP still trades unconnected nets for clearance/courtyard errors, because the snap packs against the IC and a narrow board has no room to absorb it. Relevant to the dual decision — a dual at ~10-12 HP may land in the width where this actually routes.

comments.author: Avery Wagar
comments.text:
RE-MEASURED 2026-07-27 (late), on branch layout/determinism-fab-gate-silk, real puget-hardware netlist, LOB_PARTS_DIR=~/src/puget-hardware/.lob/parts. STILL NOT FAB-READY, and the numbers are WORSE than the 11:22 comment above.

lob fab slew_limiter — the actual gate:
  auto panel 6 HP (declared 5 HP spec is stale, missing SW1 — see [[legion-of-bom-m1b]], reproducing live)
  seeded layout (analog), 6 attempts, signal HPWL 469mm, critical 63mm, 24 vias
  5 unrouted: GND->C2.2, N$3->U2.9, N$3->R7.1, RATE_CV->RV1.2, SLEW_BUF->U2.5
  12 DRC errors: 5x unconnected, 2x pth_inside_courtyard, 2x solder_mask_bridge, 2x clearance, 1x shorting_items
  -> 'refusing to build a fab package'

hp_search width sweep (its own derived panel, so not directly comparable to the fab path):
   6 HP · 16 errors (10x unconnected)
   8 HP ·  8 errors (3x unconnected)
  10 HP ·  8 errors (5x unconnected)
  nothing in range built clean

DETERMINISTIC: 10 HP re-run twice, byte-identical result. So this is not run-to-run noise.

DISCREPANCY, NOT YET ATTRIBUTED. The 11:22 comment reports 10 HP at 1 unconnected and 'one DRC error from clean'; today's sweep says 5 unconnected and 8 errors. I cannot tell from the bead which harness produced the 11:22 figures, so I am NOT calling this a regression — but one of the two measurements is not measuring what it claims, and that needs settling before any width decision is made on top of it.

STRONG HYPOTHESIS: the RANGE switch. SW1 is new enough that the declared panel predates it, and the shorting error is on RANGE_GLIDE (nets GND and RANGE_GLIDE). crate::summing fixed CTRL_FB/CTRL_SUM as claimed — neither appears in today's unrouted list — so the summing-node work HELD, and what is blocking now is [[legion-of-bom-e7k]] (does not route clean with the RANGE switch). Worth confirming by building the netlist with SW1 removed and comparing.

comments.author: Avery Wagar
comments.text:
ROUTING IS NOT THE BLOCKER — measured, not argued (2026-07-27).

I built the negotiated-congestion router the earlier analysis called for (PathFinder, McMurchie & Ebeling FPGA'95) and A/B'd it against GridRouter on this board at a FIXED placement, so the router is the only variable:

  6 HP  (declared panel): unrouted 4->2,   DRC 8->6
  8 HP:                   unrouted 16->14, DRC 9->6
  10 HP:                  tie
  6 HP  (auto panel — what lob fab actually builds): unrouted 10->9, DRC 16->15

It is a genuinely better router: better or tied everywhere, with less copper and fewer vias. And it moves this board from 12 DRC errors to 13 end-to-end. That is the finding.

So the hypothesis that a rip-up router would unblock the slew limiter is WRONG, and the earlier note in this bead saying 'the answer is either more HP or a real rip-up router' can be closed out: more HP does not help (measured), and a real rip-up router does not help (measured). Both of the two proposed answers are now ruled out by experiment.

What is left is upstream of routing: the RANGE switch ([[legion-of-bom-e7k]] — the shorting error is on RANGE_GLIDE), and the stale declared panel that makes the board build at a width nobody chose ([[legion-of-bom-m1b]]). Next cheap experiment remains the one already proposed: build the netlist with SW1 removed and compare.

comments.author: Avery Wagar
comments.text:
REOPENED — my 'fab-ready' close was WRONG, caught by the user looking at the board 2026-07-28.

I closed this on 'DRC: 0 errors' and a written fab package. But KiCad DRC HAS NO 'footprint outside the board outline' RULE — this repo already knew that ([[kicad-drc-cannot-see-a-part-off-the-board]], measured 2026-07-26) and I used a 0-DRC result as proof of fab-readiness anyway.

The board I called shippable, measured directly against its own Edge.Cuts:
    U1 copper sticks out 6.50mm past the LEFT edge  (an entire SOIC-16 hanging off)
    C2 copper sticks out 0.50mm past the BOTTOM edge

And OUR OWN RULES SAY SO. rules_report on that exact board:
    [physical]  -9.0mm  U1 hangs 9.0mm past the board's 1.5mm edge clearance
    [physical]  -3.0mm  C2 hangs 3.0mm past the board's 1.5mm edge clearance

So the rule is derived correctly, evaluated correctly, and reported correctly — and lob fab wrote the package anyway. See the new P0.

ALSO VISIBLE, same root: the placement is shifted ~6.5mm LEFT of the outline. Parts occupy x 126.76..157.78; the board is 133.26..163.74. That is U1 off the left edge AND a 5.96mm dead strip down the right-hand side, which is what the user noticed independently. One displacement, two symptoms.

comments.author: Avery Wagar
comments.text:
STATE OF THE REAL BOARD, 2026-07-28, measured while doing [[legion-of-bom-unc]].
This bead's title is out of date twice over: the board is 6 HP now (5 HP was
never buildable), and it is clean.

  lob fab slew_limiter (derived 6 HP panel)   0 DRC errors, 15 warnings
  lob fab slew_limiter (derived 8 HP panel)   0 DRC errors, 10 warnings
                                             (was REFUSED before today — see
                                              [[legion-of-bom-3kf]])

And the "byte-identical at 6/8/10/12 HP" observation recorded here does not
reproduce on the derived panel. It came from feeding route_bench the DECLARED
5 HP panel with an --hp override, which keeps every cutout at x=12.7 whatever
the board width — so the anchors, and therefore the whole placement, genuinely
could not respond to width. With the panel derived at each width (which is what
lob fab actually builds), the placements differ at every HP; measured with
crates/core/examples/place_probe.rs:
  4 HP  front 41.3% / back 17.1%, 2 parts overflow (C5, U1)
  6 HP  front 27.5% / back 11.4%, none
  8 HP  front 20.6% / back  8.6%, none
So the packer does respond to width. What it could not do was reconsider a
part's pose or its own commit order — both now addressed, see unc.

hp_search now agrees with the real build, which it did not this morning:
6 HP DRC clean from both. (That agreement is not mine — toggling my five edits
off leaves it clean too; it came from other work landed today.)

title: [bug] slew_limiter board is built wider than its own panel (30.4mm board vs 5 HP / 25.4mm panel)
description:
MISFILED — the build is doing the right thing. Retitled in effect: the defect is
in the DASHBOARD, not the board.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENS. slew_limiter_panel.toml declares hp = 5. minimum_hp says
the parts need 6 HP. `effective_panel` (cli/src/main.rs) detects that the
declared panel is stale for exactly that reason —

    declared.hp (5) < min_hp (6)  ->  "5 HP, but the PCB needs 6 HP"

— refuses to overwrite the author's tracked file (deliberately, per
[[legion-of-bom-byh]]), writes a substitute to
out/slew_limiter/slew_limiter_auto_panel.toml with hp = 6, builds against that,
and prints a warning. Verified: that file exists, says hp = 6, and carries the
same 20:26 mtime as the board. So the 30.4mm board is a 6 HP board built against
a 6 HP derived panel. Nothing silently widened anything.

THE REAL DEFECT: crates/core/src/project.rs:191 reads panel HP from
`c.panel_path(root)` — the DECLARED spec — so the dashboard prints "Panel · 5 HP"
next to a board built at 6 HP, with no sign that a substitution happened. That
mislabel is what made this look like a board/panel mismatch and cost an hour of
investigation. The build's warning goes to the transcript; the dashboard shows
none of it.

FIX (small, no placement risk): when out/<stem>/<stem>_auto_panel.toml exists it
is the panel the last build actually used — report its HP, and surface that it
differs from the declared spec. Same resolution the build already does, applied
to the view. Note write_auto_panel is also the no-declared-panel path, where the
substitute IS the panel and the dashboard currently shows nothing at all.

FOR THE USER, SEPARATELY: slew_limiter_panel.toml should be updated to 6 HP (or
the board made to fit 5). Right now every build re-derives the substitute and
warns.
close_reason:
ROOT-CAUSED and FIXED 2026-07-28. The board and the panel resolved their spec by DIFFERENT routes:

  lob fab / lob guide  -> effective_panel(): detects the declared spec is stale (missing SW1), leaves it untouched, derives a substitute and builds against that -> 6 HP
  lob panel pcb <spec> -> read the file, plot it verbatim. No circuit in scope, so no way to notice -> 5 HP

Same inputs, two answers, neither complaining. On the slew limiter that is a 25.40mm panel for a 30.48mm board — a module that cannot be assembled, and exactly what the user was looking at when they said 'the 5 HP version'.

FIX: lob panel pcb now resolves its argument the way every other command does (the resolve_circuit idiom). An existing FILE is still plotted as given — an ad-hoc spec has no circuit to check against, and that case must keep working. A NAME goes through the manifest, reads the CACHED netlist (offline, no SKiDL run, because a panel is plotted far more often than a circuit changes) and applies the same effective_panel staleness check the board build applies. No cached netlist means it says so and plots unchecked rather than failing.

VERIFIED:
  lob panel pcb slew_limiter                       -> 30.48 x 128.50mm (6 HP), 6 cutouts, matches the board
  lob panel pcb circuits/.../slew_limiter_panel.toml -> 25.40mm (5 HP), 5 cutouts, unchanged ad-hoc behaviour

STILL TRUE AND SEPARATE: the declared spec really is stale. The fix stops the two artifacts disagreeing; it does not author the missing SW1 cutout. Either fix the declared spec or drop 'panel =' and adopt the derived one — which is what the warning has always said.

title: [bug] board generation was nondeterministic: routing input came out of a HashMap
description:
FOUND while measuring [[legion-of-bom-d8t]]: the same binary on the same netlist
produced two different boards depending on the run. On daisy_panel_demo, 179
tracks / 0 conflicts or 191 tracks / 2 conflicts -- a score of 311.5 or 412.4.

Placement and legalization were bit-identical every run; the divergence was in
the router, and the cause was upstream of it in board.rs:

    let mut nets: Vec<RouteNet> = net_pads.into_values().collect();

`net_pads` is a HashMap, `into_values()` hands them over in hash order, and Rust
reseeds hash iteration PER PROCESS. GridRouter::route sorts by net index, so the
routing ORDER was already deterministic -- but route_pass paints every net's pads
and clearance halo into the grid in the order it is given, and where two halos
overlap the last writer owns the cell. Different obstacle map, different route.

FIXED, two places:
  board.rs   nets.sort_by_key(|n| n.net_idx) before routing
  route.rs   the rip-up loop iterated `blame` (HashMap<usize, HashSet<usize>>)
             to accumulate ordering constraints, and that loop skips a
             constraint whose reverse is already present -- so visiting in a
             different order accumulates a DIFFERENT constraint set. Sorted.

The second one alone did not fix it; both were needed.

WHY IT MATTERED. The whole layout loop is built on "deterministic shake -- no
RNG -- so each attempt is a clean, reproducible git diff" (layout.rs), and
route.rs's own comment claims "ties break the same way every run and the same
board comes out twice". Neither was true for any board dense enough to need
rip-up. It also silently poisoned placer A/B measurements.

NOT UNIT-TESTABLE in-process: two HashMaps built the same way in one process
iterate the same way, so a test that calls route() twice cannot catch this. The
check is to run the process twice and compare -- `place_bench` now prints a
placement fingerprint for exactly that, and board_preview writing byte-identical
.kicad_pcb files twice is the end-to-end version.
close_reason: fixed: sorted the routing net list by net index, and sorted the rip-up blame iteration

title: placement: replace greedy centroid with analytical (quadratic) global placement
description:
ARCHITECTURE AUDIT, prompted by the user asking whether anything is over-complex or fixable by changing approach rather than brute force. It is, and this is it.

SeededPlacer is a GREEDY CENTROID placer: place each free part at the weighted centroid of what it is netted to, one at a time, committing as it goes. It cannot trade one constraint against another, because by the time it sees the second constraint the first is already committed.

Everything built on top is a patch for that:
  DECOUPLE_PULL 12.0    bypass caps landed across the board
  decouple::snap        ...so a whole pass to move them back to the power pin
  Rule::Separation      panel hardware overlapped
  legalize              ...so a pass to push it apart
  repair_nudges x6      shake the free parts and re-score, hoping
  FEEDBACK_PULL         feedback network scattered (RA 45mm from U2)

43 references to pull/bonus/nudge/snap across board.rs, layout.rs, decouple.rs. Each patch is individually justified. Collectively they are compensating for the global stage.

EVIDENCE THAT PATCHING HAS RUN OUT: the FEEDBACK_PULL attempt today went 5 DRC errors -> 7 and broke a CRITICAL net. Greedy satisfied one strong pull and then painted itself into a corner. Reverted. See [[legion-of-bom-yck]].

THE LITERATURE, from our own [[legion-of-bom-957]]: "An analytical approach and fine-tuning strategy for PCB placement optimization" gives the three-stage architecture global -> legalization -> fine-tuning. Legalization landed this session; fine-tuning is the layout loop. Stage 1 is the one still greedy.

Quadratic placement minimises sum(w_ij * d_ij^2) by solving a sparse linear system: all constraints at once, no commit order, and the squared term punishes long HIGH-WEIGHT edges hardest -- which is exactly the decoupling and feedback cases, without a special case for either.

WHAT IT WOULD LET US DELETE: decouple::snap (the pull would be enough), FEEDBACK_PULL as a separate idea, most of repair_nudges. legalize STAYS -- it is stage 2 and analytical placement produces overlaps by construction.

KEEP AS-IS: rules-as-data with tiers matches the constraint-driven lineage (Malavasi 1996); topology-derived constraints are what ALIGN does, and decoupling_pairs is that in miniature.

RELATED: [[legion-of-bom-8k8]] (Steiner instead of HPWL in the score) is the objective-function half of the same question.
close_reason: landed: crates/core/src/analytical.rs; SeededPlacer solves instead of seeding. Slew limiter now first-pass DRC-clean (was 4 unrouted/6 DRC). Follow-ups: legion-of-bom-7a7, legion-of-bom-lso

comments.author: Avery Wagar
comments.text:
LANDED. crates/core/src/analytical.rs is stage one; SeededPlacer now solves
instead of seeding. Measured single-pass (max_iters=1, no repair) against the
greedy placer, both with the determinism fix from [[legion-of-bom-gns]] applied,
across every netlist in out/:

  slew_limiter (8HP, 5 anchors)  711.9 / 4 unrouted / 6 DRC  ->  553.4 / 0 / 0
  vbom_demo_circuit               46.6  ->  35.1
  opamp_noninv                    43.6  ->  36.3
  rc_ladder                       32.4  ->  30.8
  double_sided                    32.6  ->  30.2
  rectifier                       22.9  ->  19.1
  rc_lowpass                      11.3  ->   9.7
  daisy_demo                      27.5  ->  27.5  (tie)
  daisy_panel_demo               257.2  -> 412.4  (REGRESSION, see below)
  patch_sm / seed2_dfm / dfm_fanout: unchanged (all already failing DRC)

The headline is the slew limiter: the shipped 8 HP board comes out routable and
KiCad-DRC-clean on the FIRST placement, where greedy needed the repair loop's
second attempt to get there. Through the full loop both are clean and greedy
still scores 2.6% better (539.1 vs 553.4) -- greedy's nudged second attempt
happens to find a slightly tighter arrangement. Robustness bought, ~3% of
wirelength paid.

WHAT THE BEAD GOT RIGHT
  * Greedy could not trade constraints; solving all of them at once fixes the
    class of failure that [[legion-of-bom-yck]] hit.
  * legalize stays -- analytical placement overlaps by construction.

WHAT THE BEAD GOT WRONG
  * "delete decouple::snap -- the pull would be enough". MEASURED: it is not.
    Without snap the slew limiter puts C3 26.4mm from U2 against a 6.7mm rule
    (rule penalty 22198). decouple.rs was right in its own doc: "against this
    pin" is a position, not a pull. snap STAYS.
  * DECOUPLE_PULL could not stay at 12.0. Under greedy it was a hint that broke
    ties; a solver OBEYS it, and at 12.0 three bypass caps outweigh the entire
    signal path -- 4 unrouted, 6 DRC. Swept: 2.5-3.5 all clean, now 3.0.
  * repair_nudges are untouched -- still the fine-tuning stage, and the loop
    still uses them when the first placement is not clean.

TWO THINGS THE LITERATURE MADE US ADD
  * One solve is not enough. A single quadratic solve is COLLAPSED: on the slew
    board it asks for every free part inside a 1.7 x 44mm sliver of a 40 x 128mm
    board. Added SimPL's (Kim/Lee/Markov ICCAD 2012) lower/upper-bound walk:
    pack the collapsed answer, re-solve with pseudo-anchors at the packed
    positions, ramp their strength. Rounds=0 leaves a DRC error on the slew
    board; it converges by round 2.
  * A board with NOTHING anchored has no boundary condition at all, and every
    part falls back to `home`. Answering that with one point knots the whole
    circuit in the middle of the board -- that is what cost daisy_panel_demo 3
    unrouted nets before per-part homes (an even spread) went in.

Also tried and REJECTED on evidence: gauge-fixing the unanchored case by pinning
the most-connected part. Principled (Phi is translation-invariant) but lost on 7
of 10 circuits. Not kept.

comments.author: Avery Wagar
comments.text: REVERTED. See [[legion-of-bom-10k]]: on the real 5 HP puget-hardware slew limiter the analytical placer broke a physical rule (penalty 1e6, J3 past edge clearance, 9 DRC errors vs 6) and put U1 6.5mm off the board edge. SeededPlacer is greedy centroid again. crates/core/src/analytical.rs stays in the tree, wired to nothing, so the work is recoverable.

title: DRC gate could read a stale report from a previous run
description:
FOUND AND FIXED, filed because it invalidated measurements.

run_drc wrote its JSON to std::env::temp_dir()/lob-<stem>-drc.json and never cleared it first. layout::drc_on wrote every board to temp_dir()/lob_layout_<circuit>.kicad_pcb -- one path, reused for every candidate width in an HP search. So any kicad-cli hiccup meant the PREVIOUS widths report was read as the current ones result.

Symptom: the slew limiter at 7 HP returned 2 errors, then 6, then 4, on identical input. board_preview was byte-identical across runs, which is what localised it to the search path rather than to placement or routing.

FIX: remove the report before invoking kicad-cli, and stamp each boards temp path with a hash of its own contents. Three runs now give 6/6/6.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE ANNOYANCE: any DRC count quoted before this fix could have been a different widths. In particular I reported "7 HP -> 2 errors, placement errors gone" while working [[legion-of-bom-lau]] and that was a stale read; the honest number at the time was 6, all unconnected. Re-measured everything after the fix.

Related: [[legion-of-bom-nz1]] was the same species of problem -- a harness whose measurements did not mean what they appeared to.

title: Imported circuits' build guides have no board images
description: An imported circuit's build guide contains no board imagery at all. A source-built one's does. Same command (lob build), same repo. Measured: circuit origin guide size base64
acceptance_criteria: An imported circuit's guide shows the board for each step, as a source-built circuit's does.

title: V-BOM is not kit-aware: lists SMD parts JLCPCB already soldered
description:
The build guide filters to the parts a customer actually places. The V-BOM does
not, so a through-hole kit ships a sorting sheet full of SMD passives the buyer
will never touch.

Measured on tvca (imported Super Synthesis circuit, out/tvca/):

  tvca-guide.html  CORRECT  "Through-hole kit - SMD pre-assembled", 4 steps, 9 parts
  tvca-vbom.html   WRONG    "Component sorting sheet", 44 components / 16 distinct,
                            including C10-C15 100nF 0603 and C1/C3 10uF 1206

The sheet even instructs "Lay each component on its cell; the resistor bands and
package outlines are drawn life-size" - for 0603 parts that arrive pre-soldered
on the back of the board. It is the factory's view of the BOM presented as the
customer's.

These products are: JLCPCB assembles the SMD, the buyer solders the through-hole
panel hardware. lob.toml already encodes that as kit = "mixed" on the
source-built circuits, and the guide honours it.

Two things make this impossible to work around from outside lob:

1. "lob build" has no --kit flag. It reads lob.toml, which is fine, but the
   imported circuits (phrsr, scanner, tvca, eg, 2opfm) declare no kit and fall
   through to [defaults] kit = "auto", which detects from pad types and sees an
   SMD board.

2. "lob guide <imported>" refuses outright: 'tvca' is an imported circuit (fab
   package only) - it has no source to build from. So guide and V-BOM for
   imported circuits derive from the JLCPCB fab package, which is inherently an
   SMD assembly BOM, and there is no way to request a THT-filtered version even
   by hand.

Suggested fix: the V-BOM should apply the same kit filter the guide already
applies, so "mixed" yields a sorting sheet of only the parts the buyer places.
Likely in crates/core/src/bom.rs (or wherever the sorting sheet is assembled) -
the guide path clearly already has the predicate.

Found while publishing support docs from elmers (puget/module-docs). Downstream
is unblocked and shipping; the published pages just currently link a V-BOM that
overstates the work. Live example:
https://files.puget.audio/support/OSS-TVCA/0.0.1/vbom.html
acceptance_criteria: A mixed/THT kit V-BOM lists only the parts the buyer places - tvca shows 9, matching its guide, not 44.

title: router: pure Manhattan, no 45-degree segments, and via-heavy
description:
User: "our router is not ideal at all. Looking at the traces on the SuperSynthesis stuff it is much cleaner than our spaghetti." Correct, and measurable.

MEASURED on a generated slew_limiter board, read from our own .kicad_pcb (segment entries only, so no pour contamination):

  direction   100% H/V, 0% at 45 degrees
  vias        46 across 18 routed nets = 2.6 vias PER NET
  segments    219, 926mm copper

GridRouter is a Manhattan maze router: every turn is 90 degrees. Hand-routed and good autorouted boards chamfer corners at 45, which is most of what "clean vs spaghetti" actually means visually. Zero diagonals is a property of the router, not of the board.

2.6 vias per net on a 14-part circuit is the other half. A hand-routed 2-layer board this size runs 10-20 vias TOTAL. Every via is a layer change the maze router took because it could not get past an obstacle in-plane.

CAVEAT ON THE COMPARISON: I tried to measure the SuperSynthesis boards for contrast and could NOT get trustworthy numbers. DipTrace emits only two draw apertures (0.254mm and 0.508mm) and uses them for BOTH traces and ground-pour fill, so segment counts and copper lengths off those gerbers are meaningless -- tvca top reads 7644 segments / 9.9m of copper, which is nearly all pour. Their 61/39 H-V-to-45 split is suggestive but not clean either. Do not quote those numbers.

WORK:
  1. 45-degree routing. Post-process corners into chamfers at minimum; better, let the maze search move diagonally.
  2. Via reduction: prefer in-plane detours over layer changes, and a rip-up/retry pass so a via is a last resort rather than a first move. Overlaps [[legion-of-bom-yck]].
  3. Layer-directional preference (H on one side, V on the other) is the classic 2-layer discipline and falls out of 1+2.

This is likely also why [[legion-of-bom-e7k]] will not route clean -- and it means MORE HP IS NOT THE FIX. Front-side fill on that board is 22-29%; the board is not full, the router is just bad at using it.
notes:
DONE. 8-connected search with an octile heuristic and corner-cut prevention, plus via cost 2.0 -> 10.0mm swept empirically (new examples/viasweep).

Measured end to end on the slew limiter:
  before  219 segments  926mm copper  46 vias   0% diagonal
  after   246 segments  856mm copper  28 vias  52% diagonal

Copper -8%, vias -39%. Remaining router work if wanted: layer-directional preference (H on one side, V on the other), and rip-up/retry which is [[legion-of-bom-yck]].

NOTE it did NOT fix [[legion-of-bom-e7k]] -- that turned out to be placement.
close_reason: 45-degree copper and a swept via cost. 926->856mm copper, 46->28 vias, 0%->52% diagonal on the slew limiter. See the note for the numbers and what is left.

title: slew limiter does not route clean with the RANGE switch
description:
Blocks ordering the slew limiter PCBA. ERC is clean and the panel derives correctly, but no width routes DRC-clean:

  4 HP  8 errors  2x solder_mask_bridge 2x unconnected 1x clearance 1x courtyards_overlap 1x pth_inside_courtyard 1x shorting
  5 HP  6 errors
  6 HP  9 errors  (6x unconnected)
  7 HP  10 errors

PRIME SUSPECT: SW1 carries a PLACEHOLDER footprint. KiCad ships no THT sub-mini toggle, so it uses Connector_PinHeader_2.54mm:PinHeader_1x03_P2.54mm_Vertical. Its outline is 3.54 x 8.62mm; the real Dailywell 2M body is 9.14 x 8.13mm -- 2.4x the area. The placer is packing around a switch far smaller than the one that will be soldered on, so the layout is OPTIMISTIC and the DRC errors are probably the honest consequence, not noise. pth_inside_courtyard appearing at every width fits that.

ALSO NEW on this board: C4 (1uF) and C5 (4.7uF) are THT film, 7x2.5mm and 13x5mm, on the front with the panel hardware. On a 4-6HP board those are big parts competing with jacks and pots for front-side area.

FIX, in order:
  1. Make a real footprint for the Dailywell 2M SPDT: 3 pads at 0.100in pitch plus a courtyard matching the 9.14 x 8.13mm body and the panel bushing. Needs somewhere to live -- puget-hardware has no project footprint library yet, which is its own decision. Same class as [[legion-of-bom-65m]] (RCA) and [[legion-of-bom-pya]] (slide pot): first-use parts with no KiCad footprint.
  2. Re-run hp_search once the footprint is honest; the buildable width will likely be larger than 6 HP.
  3. If it still will not route, that is [[legion-of-bom-yck]] (router plateaus on dense 2-layer) and/or [[legion-of-bom-lau]] (single-column layout) rather than this part.

Positioning bead [[legion-of-bom-tus.11]] says compact 4-6HP; adding a switch and two film caps may break that, which is a product decision.
notes:
MORE HP IS NOT THE FIX -- withdrawing the crowding theory. Front-side fill on this board is 22-29%, so it is not full. The footprint theory is also dead: the real 9.13 x 10.14mm switch footprint now resolves from the house library and the DRC errors are unchanged.

Actual cause is almost certainly [[legion-of-bom-drk]]: the router is pure Manhattan (0% 45-degree segments) and burns 2.6 vias per net. Fix the router, not the board size.
ROOT CAUSE IS PLACEMENT, not routing and not width. Isolated by holding the width fixed and swapping the panel:

  8 HP, real slew_limiter_panel fixture (anchored)   ->  1 error  (1x unconnected)
  8 HP, derived idealised panel                      -> 12 errors (9x unconnected, plus
                                                        pth_inside_courtyard, shorting_items,
                                                        solder_mask_bridge)

Same router, same circuit, same width. The difference is entirely the placement the panel anchors produce. pth_inside_courtyard and shorting_items are placement overlaps and they appear at EVERY width with the derived panel and at NO width with the real one.

So this is [[legion-of-bom-lau]] -- the auto panel is a single centred column and degenerates once a board has six controls. hp_search inherits it, because eurorack_trial_build derives exactly that panel, which means hp_search has been grading boards that were laid out badly rather than grading widths.

With a sane panel the board is ONE unconnected net away from clean.

Router work ([[legion-of-bom-drk]]) is done and did help the copper -- 52% diagonal, -8% length, -39% vias -- but was never going to fix this.

NEXT: fix lau (multi-column / HP-aware placement), or hand-author a panel for the 6-control layout the way slew_limiter_panel.toml already is.
PANEL now fits 4 HP; the BOARD does not. Binding constraint has moved.

Narrow-panel margins (11/12 instead of 14/16) let all six controls lay out in 4 HP with 20.5mm of column spare. But minimum_hp still reports a 6 HP geometric floor for the PCB, and forcing 4 HP gives 8x copper_edge_clearance -- that is the board parts not fitting 20.32mm, nothing to do with the panel.

  4 HP  26 errors  (8x copper_edge_clearance -- PCB too narrow)
  5 HP   6 errors
  6 HP  11 errors
  7 HP  11 errors

So 4 HP is off the table for this circuit unless the BOARD gets narrower, which means the film caps (C5 is 14mm wide) and the TL074. Worth revisiting if the RANGE caps move to switched resistors -- see the discussion on [[legion-of-bom-tus.12]].

Still blocked on [[legion-of-bom-lau]]: pth_inside_courtyard and shorting_items at every width are placement overlaps from the single-column auto panel, and the same circuit on the real anchored 8 HP fixture gives 1 error.
close_reason: Closed
